questions.questionText: Your company stores large amounts of media files in Cloud Storage. After 90 days, these files are rarely accessed but must be kept for archival purposes. What is the most cost-effective and automated way to manage this data lifecycle?
options: Use a cron job on Compute Engine to copy files to a Coldline bucket.
Configure an Object Lifecycle Management rule to transition objects to Coldline storage after 90 days.
Enable Object Versioning and delete the original files after 90 days.
Set a Retention Policy of 90 days on the bucket.
correctAnswers: Configure an Object Lifecycle Management rule to transition objects to Coldline storage after 90 days.

explanation.general explanation: Object Lifecycle Management in Cloud Storage allows you to define rules that automatically trigger actions, such as changing an object's storage class to a colder, cheaper tier (like Coldline) when conditions like age (90 days) are met.

why other options are wrong.Use a cron job on Compute Engine to copy: Using custom compute resources and scripts creates unnecessary operational overhead when a native, free lifecycle management feature exists.
why other options are wrong.Enable Object Versioning and delete the: Object Versioning keeps old copies when modified/deleted, which increases storage costs rather than transitioning data to cheaper tiers.
why other options are wrong.Set a Retention Policy of 90 days on the: A Retention Policy prevents data from being deleted or modified for 90 days; it does not transition the storage class to save money.

questions.questionText: A healthcare application stores patient records in Cloud Storage. Regulatory requirements dictate that these files cannot be deleted or modified by anyone for exactly 7 years. Which feature must you configure to enforce this retention requirement?
options: Bucket Lock with a 7-year Retention Policy
correctAnswers: Bucket Lock with a 7-year Retention Policy

explanation.general explanation: A Retention Policy governs how long objects in a bucket must be retained. When you lock the policy using Bucket Lock, it becomes immutable, ensuring data cannot be deleted or modified for the specified period, satisfying WORM compliance.

why other options are wrong.Uniform Bucket-Level Access: This feature unifies access control via IAM but does not prevent authorized users from deleting files.
why other options are wrong.Object Lifecycle Management: Lifecycle management automates transitions or deletions, but it does not mathematically prevent users from manually deleting the files before 7 years.
why other options are wrong.Customer-Managed Encryption Keys (CMEK): CMEK secures data at rest but has no impact on retention policies or preventing deletion.

questions.questionText: Your data science team frequently creates temporary tables in a specific BigQuery dataset for intermediate processing. These tables clutter the dataset and consume storage costs. What is the easiest way to ensure any new table created in this dataset is automatically deleted after 30 days?
options: Configure the 'Default table expiration' setting on the dataset to 30 days.
Use a Cloud Function triggered by Cloud Scheduler to drop tables daily.
Set up an Object Lifecycle Management rule on the underlying storage.
Assign a Time-to-Live (TTL) field within each table's schema.
correctAnswers: Configure the 'Default table expiration' setting on the dataset to 30 days.

explanation.general explanation: BigQuery datasets have a 'Default table expiration' property. If set, any new table created in the dataset will automatically inherit this expiration time (e.g., 30 days) and be deleted automatically, eliminating manual cleanup and reducing costs.

why other options are wrong.Use a Cloud Function triggered by Cloud: This introduces unnecessary custom code and maintenance when BigQuery supports this natively.
why other options are wrong.Set up an Object Lifecycle Management ru: BigQuery storage is managed by Google; you cannot apply Cloud Storage OLM rules directly to BigQuery tables.
why other options are wrong.Assign a Time-to-Live (TTL) field within: While Firestore uses TTL fields, BigQuery table expiration is set at the table metadata or dataset level, not as a schema field.

questions.questionText: A financial application writes high-frequency trading metrics to Cloud Bigtable. To manage storage costs, the business only needs to retain the last 5 updates (versions) for any given cell. Which Bigtable feature should you configure?
options: A Garbage Collection policy based on 'max versions'.
A Garbage Collection policy based on 'max age'.
correctAnswers: A Garbage Collection policy based on 'max versions'.

explanation.general explanation: Cloud Bigtable manages data retention using Garbage Collection policies. A 'max versions' policy automatically deletes older versions of a cell's data once the number of versions exceeds the specified limit (e.g., keeping only the last 5 updates).

why other options are wrong.A Garbage Collection policy based on 'ma: Max age deletes data based on time (e.g., older than 30 days), whereas the requirement is specifically to retain a specific number of updates (versions).
why other options are wrong.Object Lifecycle Management with 'numNew: This is a Cloud Storage feature, not a Cloud Bigtable feature.
This applies to BigQuery to delete an entire table, not specific cell versions in Bigtable.

questions.questionText: When configuring Cloud Storage Object Lifecycle Management, which of the following are valid 'Actions' that can be triggered when a condition is met? (Select two)

explanation.general explanation: Cloud Storage Object Lifecycle Management currently supports a specific set of actions. The primary actions are `SetStorageClass` (to move objects to colder storage like Nearline or Archive) and `Delete` (to permanently remove the object).

why other options are wrong.Compress: Cloud Storage does not natively compress objects via lifecycle rules.
why other options are wrong.Encrypt: Encryption is handled by default at rest or via CMEK/CSEK during upload, not as a post-upload lifecycle action.
why other options are wrong.MoveToDatabase: Lifecycle rules cannot natively export objects to a database; they only manage the object's state within Cloud Storage.

questions.questionText: Your team uses a Cloud Storage bucket for collaborative document editing. To safeguard against a user accidentally overwriting a critical configuration file, which storage feature should you enable?

explanation.general explanation: Object Versioning retains a noncurrent version of an object each time it is replaced or deleted. This allows you to easily restore a file if it is accidentally overwritten or deleted by a user.

why other options are wrong.Bucket Lock: Bucket Lock makes data immutable and prevents deletion entirely, which would break the normal collaborative editing (overwriting) workflow.
why other options are wrong.Uniform Bucket-Level Access: This simplifies IAM permissions but does not protect against accidental overwrites by authorized users.
why other options are wrong.Cloud Storage FUSE: This allows mounting buckets as file systems but does not provide historical version recovery.

questions.questionText: You are migrating a legal discovery application to GCP. Legal documents must be placed on a 'Legal Hold', which prevents them from being deleted or modified indefinitely until the legal case is closed. Which Cloud Storage feature meets this requirement?

explanation.general explanation: A Temporary Hold is an object-level retention feature in Cloud Storage. While applied, the object cannot be deleted or replaced. It is typically used for legal and regulatory purposes and can be removed at any time when the hold is no longer needed.

why other options are wrong.Object Lifecycle Management: This feature automates transitions and deletions; it does not place manual compliance holds on objects.
why other options are wrong.Event-based Hold: An Event-based Hold pauses a retention policy countdown until the hold is removed (e.g., waiting for an event to occur), whereas a Temporary Hold simply prevents deletion indefinitely on its own.
why other options are wrong.Customer-Managed Encryption Keys: Encryption keys secure data privacy, not data retention or deletion prevention.

questions.questionText: You are using a time-partitioned table in BigQuery to store daily log data. You want to automatically discard log entries that are older than 90 days to minimize storage costs. What should you configure?
options: Set the partition expiration time to 90 days.
Set the dataset default table expiration to 90 days.
Write a daily scheduled query to run `DELETE FROM table WHERE date < CURRENT_DATE() - 90`.
Set an Object Lifecycle rule on the BigQuery backing storage.
correctAnswers: Set the partition expiration time to 90 days.

explanation.general explanation: For time-partitioned tables in BigQuery, setting the 'partition expiration time' ensures that Google automatically deletes individual partitions (e.g., specific days of log data) once they exceed the specified age, providing a zero-maintenance lifecycle policy.

why other options are wrong.Set the dataset default table expiration: This would delete the *entire table* 90 days after it was created, rather than dropping old data rows on a rolling basis.
why other options are wrong.Write a daily scheduled query to run `DE: While possible, DML operations (DELETE) consume compute resources and incur costs. Partition expiration is native, automatic, and free.
why other options are wrong.Set an Object Lifecycle rule on the BigQ: BigQuery storage is managed internally; you cannot access its underlying files to apply Cloud Storage OLM rules.

questions.questionText: When setting up Object Lifecycle Management (OLM) rules in Cloud Storage, you can combine multiple conditions to trigger an action. Which of the following are valid OLM conditions? (Select three)

explanation.general explanation: Cloud Storage OLM supports several conditions to trigger actions. Common conditions include 'Age' (time since creation), 'MatchesStorageClass' (applies only if the object is in a specific class), and 'NumNewerVersions' (useful for managing versioned objects).

why other options are wrong.FileSizeInBytes: Cloud Storage OLM does not currently support triggering rules based directly on the file size in bytes.
why other options are wrong.FileExtension: OLM uses `MatchesPrefix` and `MatchesSuffix` (which can act like an extension check), but the exact condition name is not 'FileExtension'.

questions.questionText: You are building a real-time web application using Firestore. The application stores temporary user session data that must be automatically deleted 24 hours after the session is created. Which feature should you implement?
options: Cloud Scheduler invoking a Cloud Function

explanation.general explanation: Firestore supports Time-to-Live (TTL) policies. By defining a TTL policy on a specific timestamp field in your documents, Firestore will automatically delete the documents in the background after the timestamp has expired, without any custom code.

why other options are wrong.Cloud Scheduler invoking a Cloud Functio: While you could write a script to do this, native TTL policies are more robust, fully managed, and cost-effective.
why other options are wrong.Object Lifecycle Management: This is a feature of Cloud Storage, not Firestore.
why other options are wrong.Garbage Collection policies: Garbage Collection policies are used by Cloud Bigtable, not Firestore.

questions.questionText: Your organization has a strict data retention policy requiring that log files be stored for 5 years. After the first 6 months, these logs are almost never accessed. Which Cloud Storage storage class should you target with your lifecycle rule to minimize costs over the 5-year period?

explanation.general explanation: The Archive storage class offers the lowest storage cost for data that is accessed less than once a year. Since the logs must be kept for 5 years but are rarely accessed after 6 months, an OLM rule transitioning them to Archive is the most cost-effective choice.

why other options are wrong.Standard: Standard is the most expensive storage class, designed for frequently accessed data.
why other options are wrong.Nearline: Nearline is designed for data accessed roughly once a month, which is more expensive than Archive.
why other options are wrong.Coldline: Coldline is designed for data accessed roughly once a quarter. Archive is cheaper for data kept for years without access.

questions.questionText: You have a Cloud Storage bucket with Object Versioning enabled. You want to save costs by permanently deleting any noncurrent version of an object after it has been noncurrent for 30 days. Which condition and action should you use in your lifecycle rule?

explanation.general explanation: The `DaysSinceNoncurrentTime` condition specifies the number of days since an object became noncurrent (i.e., a newer version was uploaded or the object was deleted). Using this with the `Delete` action cleans up old versions specifically.

why other options are wrong.Action: SetStorageClass, Condition: Age=: This transitions the storage class based on creation age, not deletion of noncurrent versions.
why other options are wrong.Action: Delete, Condition: Age=30: This would delete the current, live version of the object 30 days after it was created, which is not the goal.
why other options are wrong.Action: Delete, Condition: NumNewerVersi: This condition triggers only if there are 30 versions newer than the object, not based on the passage of 30 days.

questions.questionText: Your IoT application streams sensor data into Cloud Bigtable. The data becomes irrelevant after 30 days. How should you configure Bigtable to automatically delete this old data and save storage costs?
options: Configure a Garbage Collection policy based on a 'max age' of 30 days.
Configure Object Lifecycle Management for the instance.
Use a Cloud Function to execute row deletions every night.
Set a Time-to-Live (TTL) field on every cell.
correctAnswers: Configure a Garbage Collection policy based on a 'max age' of 30 days.

explanation.general explanation: Cloud Bigtable provides native Garbage Collection policies at the column family level. Setting a 'max age' policy of 30 days ensures that any cell older than 30 days is automatically marked for deletion and eventually removed in the background.

why other options are wrong.Configure Object Lifecycle Management fo: OLM is a feature of Cloud Storage, not Bigtable.
why other options are wrong.Use a Cloud Function to execute row dele: Manual or scripted deletions add massive compute and operational overhead compared to native garbage collection.
why other options are wrong.Set a Time-to-Live (TTL) field on every: While Firestore uses TTL, Bigtable manages expiration via Garbage Collection policies assigned to the column family.

questions.questionText: You need to ensure that temporary staging files stored in a specific Cloud Storage bucket are automatically removed exactly one year (365 days) after they are uploaded. What configuration is required?
options: Add an Object Lifecycle Management rule with Action: Delete and Condition: Age=365.
Set a Bucket Lock with a retention period of 365 days.
Enable Object Versioning with a max versions limit of 365.
Use a cron job to delete the bucket and recreate it annually.
correctAnswers: Add an Object Lifecycle Management rule with Action: Delete and Condition: Age=365.

explanation.general explanation: The most efficient, managed way to delete temporary files after a specific time is to use Cloud Storage Object Lifecycle Management. The 'Delete' action paired with the 'Age' condition (365 days) natively automates this cleanup.

why other options are wrong.Set a Bucket Lock with a retention perio: Bucket Lock prevents files from being deleted for 365 days. It does not automatically delete them once the 365 days have passed.
why other options are wrong.Enable Object Versioning with a max vers: Versioning retains modifications. Max versions is not a valid limit parameter in Cloud Storage, nor does it address age-based deletion.
why other options are wrong.Use a cron job to delete the bucket and: This is a heavy-handed, manual approach that would delete files created on day 364 just as easily as files created on day 1.

questions.questionText: BigQuery provides multiple ways to manage data retention and lifecycle automatically without custom scripting. Which of the following are native BigQuery lifecycle capabilities? (Select three)

explanation.general explanation: BigQuery natively supports lifecycle management through expiration times. You can set expiration at the dataset level (default for new tables), the table level (deleting the whole table), and the partition level (deleting old data partitions).

why other options are wrong.Object Lifecycle Management (OLM) rules: OLM is a feature of Google Cloud Storage, not BigQuery.
why other options are wrong.Bucket Lock retention policies: Bucket Lock applies to Cloud Storage buckets for WORM compliance, not to BigQuery datasets.

questions.questionText: You are managing a Cloud SQL instance. Company policy requires that daily backups of the database are retained for exactly 30 days before being deleted to minimize storage costs. How should you implement this?
options: Configure the Cloud SQL automated backups feature and set the retention limit to 30.
Export the database daily using Cloud Scheduler and use Cloud Storage OLM to delete after 30 days.
Take a manual snapshot every day and manually delete old snapshots.
Write a cron job that runs `DROP TABLE` commands for records older than 30 days.
correctAnswers: Configure the Cloud SQL automated backups feature and set the retention limit to 30.

explanation.general explanation: Cloud SQL natively supports automated daily backups and allows you to configure a retention limit (up to 365 backups). By setting the limit to 30, Cloud SQL automatically deletes older backups, completely fulfilling the requirement.

why other options are wrong.Export the database daily using Cloud Sc: While possible, this requires custom architecture (Scheduler + Functions + Storage OLM) to do something Cloud SQL does natively.
why other options are wrong.Take a manual snapshot every day and man: Manual operations are error-prone and fail to meet the automated data lifecycle best practices.
why other options are wrong.Write a cron job that runs `DROP TABLE`: This deletes the live data, not the database backups, completely violating the requirement.

questions.questionText: You have a single Cloud Storage bucket that holds both standard user images and temporary processing logs. The logs are saved with the prefix `logs/`. You want to automatically delete the logs after 7 days without affecting the user images. How do you configure this?
options: Create an OLM rule with Action: Delete, Condition: Age=7 and MatchesPrefix='logs/'.
Create a separate bucket for logs because lifecycle rules apply to the whole bucket globally.
Use a Bucket Lock with a 7-day retention policy and apply it only to the logs/ folder.
Use Object Versioning to limit the `logs/` prefix to 7 versions.
correctAnswers: Create an OLM rule with Action: Delete, Condition: Age=7 and MatchesPrefix='logs/'.

explanation.general explanation: Object Lifecycle Management rules can be targeted using conditions like `MatchesPrefix` or `MatchesSuffix`. By specifying the `logs/` prefix, the delete action will only apply to objects in that 'folder' that are 7 days old, leaving other images intact.

why other options are wrong.Create a separate bucket for logs becaus: Lifecycle rules can be scoped using prefix/suffix conditions; they do not have to apply to the entire bucket.
why other options are wrong.Use a Bucket Lock with a 7-day retention: Bucket locks apply to the entire bucket and prevent deletion; they do not trigger automated deletion.
why other options are wrong.Use Object Versioning to limit the `logs: Versioning manages object modifications, not age-based lifecycle deletion.

questions.questionText: Your mission-critical database runs on Cloud Spanner. The business requires the ability to recover the database to a specific microsecond in the past to protect against accidental data corruption or user error. What is the maximum data retention period you can configure for Cloud Spanner's Point-in-time recovery (PITR)?

explanation.general explanation: Cloud Spanner offers Point-in-time recovery (PITR) to recover data to a specific microsecond. The maximum retention period you can configure for this continuous version history is 7 days.

why other options are wrong.30 days: While Cloud SQL allows up to 35 days for PITR, Cloud Spanner's maximum limit is 7 days.
why other options are wrong.365 days: This is incorrect. Retention beyond 7 days requires taking on-demand or scheduled backups.
why other options are wrong.Unlimited: Continuous version retention consumes immense storage and is hard-capped at 7 days by Google Cloud.

questions.questionText: A law firm is migrating legal discovery files to Cloud Storage. If a case is reopened, the legal team must manually apply an indefinite lock to specific files to prevent deletion, but they need to remove this lock easily when the case concludes. Which feature allows this specific, flexible object-level retention?

explanation.general explanation: A Temporary Hold is placed on individual objects to prevent them from being deleted or replaced. It is designed for scenarios like legal discovery where a hold needs to be placed indefinitely but can be manually removed by an authorized user at any time.

why other options are wrong.Bucket Lock: Bucket Lock enforces a strict, immutable time-based retention policy on the entire bucket, which cannot be easily removed or applied on a per-object basis.
why other options are wrong.Object Versioning: Versioning keeps old copies of files but does not prevent a user from deleting those versions.
why other options are wrong.Uniform Bucket-Level Access: This is an IAM security feature, not a data retention or hold feature.

questions.questionText: When configuring a column family in Cloud Bigtable, you must define a Garbage Collection policy to manage data retention and storage costs. Which two rules can be used to define a Garbage Collection policy? (Select two)

explanation.general explanation: Cloud Bigtable Garbage Collection policies are based on two primary rules: 'Max age' (delete cells older than a certain duration) and 'Max versions' (keep only a specific number of the most recent updates for a cell).

why other options are wrong.Max byte size: Bigtable GC policies cannot be triggered based on the physical byte size of the cell.
why other options are wrong.Minimum read frequency: Bigtable does not natively delete data based on how rarely it is accessed.
why other options are wrong.Time-to-Live (TTL): While conceptually similar to max age, TTL is the terminology used by Firestore and Datastore. Bigtable specifically uses the term 'Max age' in its Garbage Collection policy.

questions.questionText: You have configured a Cloud Storage Object Lifecycle Management rule to delete objects older than 30 days. An object reaches its 30th day at 10:00 AM. A user tries to download it at 10:05 AM. What should you expect?
options: The object might still be available because lifecycle rules are executed asynchronously and may take up to 24 hours.
The object will return a 404 Not Found error because deletion is instantaneous at the exact millisecond.
The object will be downloaded, but the user will be billed double.
The object will automatically be transitioned to Coldline storage instead.
correctAnswers: The object might still be available because lifecycle rules are executed asynchronously and may take up to 24 hours.

explanation.general explanation: Object Lifecycle Management actions in Cloud Storage are not executed immediately at the exact millisecond a condition is met. Cloud Storage regularly inspects objects and performs actions asynchronously, meaning an object might still be available for up to 24 hours after meeting the condition.

why other options are wrong.The object will return a 404 Not Found e: Lifecycle execution is asynchronous, not instantaneous.
why other options are wrong.The object will be downloaded, but the u: There is no penalty billing for downloading objects pending lifecycle execution.
why other options are wrong.The object will automatically be transit: The rule is set to Delete, so it will not magically transition the storage class.

questions.questionText: Your company uses a Cloud Storage bucket with a 5-year Retention Policy. For certain loan documents, the 5-year retention countdown should only begin after the loan is officially paid off. Which feature allows you to pause the retention countdown until that business event occurs?

explanation.general explanation: An Event-based Hold pauses the retention period countdown on a specific object. Once the business event occurs (e.g., the loan is paid off), you remove the hold, and the object's retention period (e.g., 5 years) officially begins counting down from that moment.

why other options are wrong.Temporary Hold: A Temporary Hold prevents deletion but does not reset or pause a retention policy's timer in the way an Event-based hold does.
why other options are wrong.Object Versioning: Versioning keeps historical copies; it does not pause retention policy countdowns.
why other options are wrong.Object Lifecycle Management: OLM automates actions based on static conditions; it does not place holds on objects.

questions.questionText: A junior analyst accidentally ran a `DROP TABLE` command on a critical BigQuery table. Fortunately, the incident was reported 3 days later. Which built-in BigQuery feature allows you to recover this deleted table without relying on manual database exports?

explanation.general explanation: BigQuery's 'Time travel' feature allows you to access data stored in BigQuery that has been changed or deleted within the time travel window (which defaults to 7 days). You can use this to restore a deleted table easily.

why other options are wrong.Object Versioning: Object Versioning is a feature of Cloud Storage, not BigQuery.
why other options are wrong.Failover replicas: Failover replicas are used for high availability in transactional databases like Cloud SQL or Spanner, not for recovering dropped analytical tables in BigQuery.
why other options are wrong.Point-in-time recovery (PITR) via Cloud: Cloud SQL PITR cannot recover a table dropped in BigQuery.

questions.questionText: You are configuring a data lifecycle policy for a media company. The original 4K video footage needs to be stored for 10 years for compliance but will likely never be accessed again unless there is a specific legal request. Which Cloud Storage class provides the lowest storage cost for this data?

explanation.general explanation: The Archive storage class is specifically designed for data that is kept for long-term preservation (like compliance archives) and is accessed less than once a year. It offers the lowest storage cost among all Cloud Storage classes.

why other options are wrong.Coldline: Coldline is for data accessed roughly once a quarter and has a slightly higher storage cost than Archive.
why other options are wrong.Nearline: Nearline is for data accessed once a month and is more expensive than Archive.
why other options are wrong.Standard: Standard is the most expensive class, designed for frequently accessed hot data.

questions.questionText: You have configured a Time-to-Live (TTL) policy on a Firestore database to delete user session documents 2 hours after their creation. A document hits its 2-hour expiration time. How is the deletion handled by Firestore?
options: The document is deleted asynchronously by a background process, which may take up to 72 hours.
The document is deleted synchronously at the exact millisecond it expires.
The document remains until a user attempts to read it, at which point it is deleted.
The document is exported to Cloud Storage before being deleted.
correctAnswers: The document is deleted asynchronously by a background process, which may take up to 72 hours.

explanation.general explanation: Firestore TTL deletions are not instantaneous. Once the TTL expiration time is reached, the document becomes eligible for deletion. A background process sweeps and deletes expired documents, which typically happens within 72 hours.

why other options are wrong.The document is deleted synchronously at: Synchronous, instantaneous deletion is not guaranteed by TTL policies.
why other options are wrong.The document remains until a user attemp: This describes a 'lazy deletion' pattern common in caching systems (like Redis/Memcached), but Firestore sweeps them automatically in the background.
why other options are wrong.The document is exported to Cloud Storag: TTL simply deletes the document; it does not natively export it.

questions.questionText: To implement Object Lifecycle Management for a Cloud Storage bucket using Infrastructure as Code or the `gcloud` CLI, you typically define the rules in a specific structured format. Which format is used to write these lifecycle configuration files?

explanation.general explanation: When using the `gcloud storage` CLI or REST API to apply an Object Lifecycle Management configuration to a bucket, the rules and conditions are defined and passed as a JSON object.

why other options are wrong.XML: Google Cloud Storage API predominantly uses JSON for configuration payloads, not XML (though S3 interoperability uses XML, native GCP configuration uses JSON).
why other options are wrong.CSV: CSV is for tabular data, not structured configuration hierarchies.
why other options are wrong.INI: INI files are simple key-value config files and cannot express the nested arrays and objects required for complex OLM conditions.

questions.questionText: Cloud Storage provides granular object holds to satisfy legal and compliance requirements, preventing an object from being deleted. Which of the following are native types of object holds in Cloud Storage? (Select two)

explanation.general explanation: Cloud Storage supports two types of object holds: Event-based holds (which pause the retention countdown until a specific event occurs) and Temporary holds (which indefinitely prevent deletion and are often used for legal/regulatory purposes until manually removed).

why other options are wrong.Permanent hold: There is no 'Permanent hold' feature; bucket retention policies are used for strict long-term retention.
why other options are wrong.Legal hold: While Temporary holds are used *for* legal discovery, the actual technical name of the feature in GCP is 'Temporary hold'.
why other options are wrong.Version hold: This is not a valid GCP Cloud Storage feature.

questions.questionText: You have configured a Retention Policy of 1 year on a Cloud Storage bucket to satisfy WORM compliance. To ensure the policy cannot be reduced or removed by an administrator, you apply a Bucket Lock. What happens if you later realize the policy should have been 6 months?
options: You cannot reduce the retention period. A locked retention policy is irreversible and can only be increased.
You can unlock the bucket using a special CLI command.
You can request Google Support to manually override the lock.
You can delete the bucket immediately and create a new one.
correctAnswers: You cannot reduce the retention period. A locked retention policy is irreversible and can only be increased.

explanation.general explanation: Locking a retention policy (Bucket Lock) makes it permanent to meet strict regulatory WORM requirements. Once locked, the retention period cannot be reduced or removed by anyone, including Google Support. It can only be increased.

why other options are wrong.You can unlock the bucket using a specia: There is no command to unlock a bucket; the action is mathematically and administratively irreversible.
why other options are wrong.You can request Google Support to manual: Google Support does not have the ability to override a locked retention policy.
why other options are wrong.You can delete the bucket immediately an: You cannot delete a locked bucket if it contains objects whose retention periods have not yet expired.

questions.questionText: A table in BigQuery was created in a dataset that has a default table expiration of 30 days. On day 25, the team realizes this specific table contains vital data and must not be deleted. How can you preserve this specific table while keeping the dataset's default behavior for new tables?
options: Update the specific table's expiration time property to 'Never' (or a specific future date).
Remove the default table expiration from the dataset.
Create a Cloud Storage OLM rule to protect the BigQuery table.
Move the table to a Coldline dataset.
correctAnswers: Update the specific table's expiration time property to 'Never' (or a specific future date).

explanation.general explanation: When a dataset has a default table expiration, new tables inherit that expiration. However, you can update the `expirationTime` property on an individual table at any time to extend it or remove it entirely, saving it from deletion.

why other options are wrong.Remove the default table expiration from: This would affect the dataset's future behavior for new tables, which the scenario explicitly wants to keep.
why other options are wrong.Create a Cloud Storage OLM rule to prote: OLM is for Cloud Storage, not BigQuery.
BigQuery datasets do not have 'Coldline' tiers; that is a Cloud Storage concept.

questions.questionText: Your security team wants to enforce a policy where all log files uploaded to a specific Cloud Storage bucket are automatically deleted 5 years after their creation date. This policy must apply to all files in the bucket without manual intervention. Which feature handles this?

explanation.general explanation: Object Lifecycle Management is the core Cloud Storage feature used to automate data lifecycle. By setting a rule with the condition `Age=1825` (5 years) and the action `Delete`, Cloud Storage will automatically delete all objects that reach that age.

why other options are wrong.Bucket Lock: Bucket Lock enforces retention (prevents deletion) for a specified time; it does not automatically delete files once the time expires.
why other options are wrong.Event-based Hold: This pauses retention policies on specific objects based on events; it does not automate deletion.
why other options are wrong.Object Versioning: This keeps historical copies of objects when they are modified; it does not automate age-based deletion.
